issues.legal_issue: The constitutional right of a religious denomination to own property does not prevent the State from compulsorily acquiring that property under a valid acquisition law, unless the acquisition destroys or completely negates the institution’s ability to survive.
material_facts: A public religious trust held Devasthan inam lands used in connection with its religious institution.
The challenged legislation abolished the inams and extinguished associated rights as part of an agrarian reform measure.
The appellants did not allege that the changes would destroy or completely negate the institution’s ability to survive.
The Court treated acquisition in accordance with the constitutional requirements for compulsory acquisition as not assailable on any valid ground in these appeals.
issues.conclusion: The right to own property for managing religious affairs does not bar the State from acquiring that property in accordance with the constitutional requirements for compulsory acquisition; no survival-threatening acquisition was alleged in these appeals.
issues.legal_principle: Article 26(c) protects a denomination’s right to own and acquire property for managing religious affairs, but does not itself prevent compulsory acquisition satisfying Article 31(2). Once acquired, the particular property is no longer owned by the denomination. The Court followed Khajamian Wakf Estates v. State of Madras and held that it was not inconsistent with Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India, the Bank Nationalisation case. It also held that the passage in Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Shri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt concerning administration of religious affairs did not assist the appellants.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_acq: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law under which the State acquires property.
predicates.religious_institution_owns_property_for_: A religious institution owns property for the management of its religious affairs.
predicates.state_acquires_property_under_valid_law: The State acquires the institution’s property under a law that satisfies the constitutional requirements for compulsory acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_does_not_destroy_institution: The acquisition is not shown to destroy or completely negate the institution’s ability to survive.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns State acquisition of property owned by a religious institution, the State may acquire it if the acquisition meets constitutional requirements and does not destroy the institution’s ability to survive.

issues.legal_issue: A law pursuing agrarian reform may regulate property held by a religious denomination without violating its right to own property, so long as the law does not directly affect the substance of that right or the core of religious freedom.
material_facts: The legislation abolished religious and charitable institutions’ inams, extinguished associated rights, made the lands liable to land revenue, and provided for compensation.
It addressed agrarian reform and altered the treatment of land, including through provisions concerning landholders, tenants, and exemptions under agricultural legislation.
The Court found that the legislation did not directly interfere with the core of religion or affect the substance of the denominational property right.
The appellants argued that the right under Article 26(c) was not subject to the saving provision for agrarian reform because that provision did not mention Article 26.
issues.conclusion: The legislation was protected as agrarian reform and did not violate Article 26(c); the omission of Article 26 from the saving provision was immaterial because the right was not absolute and its substance was not directly affected.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 26(c), 31A, and 37, read with the Directive Principles of State Policy, informed the Court’s conclusion that a denominational property right is not absolute and must coexist with valid measures serving social welfare. The Court distinguished laws directly infringing religious freedom from laws affecting secular activities or religious institutions indirectly, and applied the principle in Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Shri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt. A court must balance competing interests; agrarian reform may regulate property without directly affecting the substance of the Article 26(c) right.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law enacted to reform agrarian arrangements.
predicates.law_regulates_land_for_social_welfare: The law changes land rights or arrangements to address social welfare concerns.
predicates.law_does_not_directly_affect_religious_f: The law does not directly interfere with religious freedom or impair the substance of the institution’s property right.

issues.definition: A law challenged as agrarian reform is saved and does not violate a denomination’s property right when it regulates land for social welfare without directly impairing religious freedom or the substance of that right.

issues.legal_issue: The adequacy of compensation cannot be challenged against legislation relating to agrarian reform that is protected by the constitutional saving provision.
material_facts: The legislation provided compensation for abolished inams and related rights.
Other provisions removed exemptions for certain religious trust lands under agricultural tenancy and land-ceiling laws.
The appellants alleged that the compensation available for lands covered by those agricultural laws was grossly inadequate.
The legislation was found to relate to agrarian reform and to be protected by the constitutional saving provision.
issues.conclusion: The objection based on inadequacy of compensation was not entertainable; objections based on Articles 14, 19, and 31 were also not entertainable against the protected agrarian-reform legislation.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A protects legislation relating to agrarian reform from specified constitutional challenges, and the Court held that an objection to the adequacy of compensation could not be agitated against legislation within that protection. The Court also stated that objections based on Articles 14, 19, and 31 were not entertainable in this context.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law enacted to reform agrarian arrangements.
predicates.law_is_protected_as_agrarian_reform: The law relates to agrarian reform and falls within the constitutional protection for such legislation.
predicates.compensation_is_challenged_as_inadequate: A party claims that the compensation provided for the effects of the law is insufficient.

issues.definition: A compensation-adequacy challenge is not entertainable when it is made against a law challenged as agrarian reform that falls within the constitutional protection for such legislation.
